For when Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart aside after other gods, and his heart was not wholly with Yahweh his God, as the heart of David his father had been.
Solomon went after Ashtoreth,{b} the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom,{c} the detestable idol of the Ammonites.
So Solomon did what was evil in Yahweh’s sight and did not follow Yahweh fully, as David his father had done.
Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh,{d} the detestable idol of Moab, on the mountain east of Jerusalem,{e} and for Molech,{f} the detestable idol of the Ammonites.
He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.
Yahweh was angry with Solomon because his heart had turned away from Yahweh, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice
and had commanded him concerning this very thing, that he should not go after other gods. But he did not keep what Yahweh commanded.

Therefore Yahweh said to Solomon, “Since this is your conduct,{g} and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I commanded you, I will surely rip the kingdom from you and hand it to your servant.
Nevertheless, in your lifetime I will not do it, for David your father’s sake; out of your son’s hand I will tear it.
Still, I will not tear away all the kingdom; one tribe I will give to your son, for David my servant’s sake and for Jerusalem’s sake, which I have chosen.”
So Yahweh stirred up an adversary{h} for Solomon: Hadad{i} the Edomite, who was of the king’s family in Edom.
For it happened, while David was in Edom and Joab, the army’s commander, had gone up to bury the dead, that he killed every male in Edom
(for Joab and all Israel stayed there six months, until he had cut off every male in Edom),
Hadad fled to Egypt with some Edomites of his father’s servants, Hadad being still a small boy.
They set out from Midian and came to Paran,{j} and they took men with them from Paran and came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave him a house, assigned him food, and gave him land.
Hadad found great favor in Pharaoh’s sight, so that he gave him as wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.
The sister of Tahpenes bore him his son Genubath, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh’s house. Genubath lived in Pharaoh’s house among Pharaoh’s sons.
But when Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers and that Joab the commander of the army was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, “Let me go, so that I may go to my own country.”
Pharaoh said to him, “What have you lacked with me, that you now want to go to your own country?” He replied, “Nothing, but please let me go.”
God also raised up another adversary against him, Rezon{k} son of Eliada, who had fled from his lord Hadadezer king of Zobah.
He gathered men around him and became leader of a raiding band, after David killed them.{l} They went to Damascus and settled there and ruled in Damascus.
He was an adversary of Israel all the days of Solomon, in addition to the harm that Hadad did. He loathed Israel and reigned over Aram.{m}
Jeroboam{n} son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah, a servant of Solomon, whose mother’s name was Zeruah, a widow, also raised his hand against the king.
This is the story of how he raised his hand against the king. Solomon had built the Millo and had closed up the breach in the city of David his father.
Jeroboam was a capable man,{o} and when Solomon saw that the young man was industrious, he put him in charge of all the forced labor of the house of Joseph.

At that time, when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah{p} the Shilonite met him on the road. Ahijah had clothed himself with a new cloak, and the two of them were alone in the open country.
Then Ahijah seized the new cloak that was on him and ripped it into twelve pieces.
And he said to Jeroboam, “Take for yourself ten pieces, because Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘See, I am tearing the kingdom from the hand of Solomon, and I will give you ten tribes.
But one tribe{q} will remain his, for David my servant’s sake and for Jerusalem’s sake, the city that I have chosen from among all Israel’s tribes.

For they have forsaken me{r} and have bowed down to Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites, and they have not walked in my ways, doing what is right in my eyes and keeping my statutes and my judgments, as David his father did.
Yet I will not take all the kingdom out of his hand. I will keep him as ruler as long as he lives, for the sake of my servant David, my chosen one, who kept my commandments and statutes.
From his son’s hand, though, I will take the kingship and give ten tribes of it to you.
And one tribe I will give to his son, so that my servant David may have a lamp{s} before me always in Jerusalem, the city I chose for myself to place my name there.
You I will take, and you will rule over everything you desire; you will be king over Israel.

If you listen to all that I command you and walk in my ways and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a lasting house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you.
So I will afflict the offspring of David for this, yet not for all time.’ ”{t}
Solomon therefore sought to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak{u} king of Egypt, and he stayed in Egypt until Solomon’s death.
The rest of the acts of Solomon, all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon?
The time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years.
Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father. And Rehoboam{v} his son reigned in his place.{w}

notes.text: The Septuagint lacks “and his wives turned his heart aside.”
Ashtoreth (Astarte) was a Canaanite goddess of fertility and war. The Hebrew vowels may have been changed to those of bosheth, “shame.”
Milcom, the national god of Ammon, a name related to melek, “king.” The Septuagint reads “their king.”
Chemosh was the national god of Moab; the meaning of the name is uncertain.
That is, the Mount of Olives; it was later called the Mount of Corruption (2 Kings 23:13).
Molech is probably another form of Milcom (verse 5; compare verse 33). The Hebrew vowels may have been changed to those of bosheth, “shame.”
Hebrew “Because this was with you.”
Hebrew satan, “adversary, opponent.”
Hadad is the name of the Aramean storm god; it may mean “thunderer.” The Septuagint calls him Ader.
Midian lay east of the Gulf of Aqaba; Paran is the wilderness south of Judah in the Sinai.
Rezon means “prince” or “ruler.” The Septuagint lacks verses 23–24 as a separate account and instead mentions Rezon (Esrom) together with Hadad in verse 14.
That is, after David defeated Hadadezer and his allies (2 Samuel 8:3–8; 10:15–19).
Aram is Syria, with its capital at Damascus.
Jeroboam may mean “may the people multiply” or “may the people contend.”
Hebrew gibbor hayil, “a mighty man of valor,” here probably of ability and standing.
Ahijah means “Yahweh is my brother.” A Shilonite is a man of Shiloh (“tranquil”?), where the tabernacle had stood.
That is, Judah, with which Benjamin was reckoned (12:21). The Septuagint reads “two tribes” here and in verse 36.
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read “he has forsaken me,” and so in the rest of the verse.
That is, a descendant on the throne; compare 15:4; 2 Kings 8:19.
The Septuagint lacks verse 39.
Shishak is Pharaoh Sheshonq I, founder of Egypt’s Twenty-second Dynasty.
Rehoboam means “the people are enlarged” or “may the people be enlarged.”
The Septuagint adds a longer account of Jeroboam’s return from Egypt here and in 12:2–3, and an alternative account of his rise at 12:24a–z.

verses.text: Rehoboam went to Shechem,{a} for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.
When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard of it (he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), Jeroboam lived on in Egypt.{b}
They sent and called him, and Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel{c} came and spoke to Rehoboam, saying,
“Your father made our yoke hard. Now lighten the hard service of your father and the heavy yoke he laid on us, and we will serve you.”
He said to them, “Go away for three days, and then come back to me.” So the people went.
King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men who had stood before Solomon his father while he was alive. “How do you advise me to answer this people?” he asked.
They told him, “If today you will be a servant to this people and serve them, and answer them by speaking kind words to them, they will be your servants forever.”
But he set aside the advice the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and who stood before him.
He asked them, “What do you advise that we answer this people, who have said to me, ‘Lighten the yoke your father put on us’?”

The young men who had grown up with him told him, “Say this to the people who told you, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us’: say to them, ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist!{d}
And now, whereas my father laid a heavy yoke on you, I will make your yoke heavier. My father punished you with whips; I will punish you with scorpions.’ ”{e}
So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam on the third day, as the king had directed, saying, “Come back to me on the third day.”
The king answered the people harshly. He set aside the counsel the old men had given him
and spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men: “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will make it heavier. My father punished you with whips; I will punish you with scorpions.”

So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of events brought about by Yahweh, so that he might fulfill his word, which Yahweh had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

When all Israel saw that the king refused to listen to them, the people gave the king this reply: “What portion is ours in David? No inheritance is ours in Jesse’s son. Back to your tents, Israel! Now see to your own house, David!” So Israel went away to their tents.
But as for the Israelites who lived in the towns of Judah, Rehoboam reigned over them.{f}
Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram,{g} the overseer of the forced labor, but all Israel pelted him with stones until he died. King Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot and fled to Jerusalem.
Thus Israel rebelled against David’s house, and so it remains to this day.
When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. No one followed the house of David except the tribe of Judah alone.

When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he assembled all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, one hundred and eighty thousand chosen warriors,{h} to fight against the house of Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam son of Solomon.
But the word of God came to Shemaiah{i} the man of God:
“Say to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin and the rest of the people,

‘This is what Yahweh says: Do not go up to make war on your kinsmen the Israelites. Return, each man to his house, because this has come about from me.’ ” So they listened to the word of Yahweh and went home again, as Yahweh had said.{j}
Jeroboam then built up Shechem in Ephraim’s hill country and made his home there; and going out from there, he built up Penuel.{k}
And Jeroboam said in his heart, “Now the kingdom will go back to the house of David.

If this people goes up to offer sacrifices in the house of Yahweh in Jerusalem, the heart of this people will turn back to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah. They will kill me and go back to Rehoboam king of Judah.”
After taking counsel, the king made two golden calves and said to the people,{l} “It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem. Look, Israel: your gods, that led you up out of Egypt’s land!”
He set one in Bethel,{m} and the other he put in Dan.{n}
This thing became a sin, for the people went as far as Dan to worship before the one there.{o}
He also made houses on high places and appointed priests from all ranks of the people, who were not of the Levites.

Jeroboam instituted a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month (October–November),{p} like the feast that was in Judah, and he went up to the altar. He did this in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves he had made, and he stationed in Bethel the priests of the high places he had made.

He went up to the altar he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, in the month that he had devised in his own heart. He instituted a feast for the Israelites and went up to the altar to burn incense.

notes.text: Shechem means “shoulder” or “ridge”; it lay between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.
So the Hebrew (wayyesheb). 2 Chronicles 10:2 and some ancient witnesses read “Jeroboam returned from Egypt” (wayyashob). The Septuagint lacks verses 2–3a here (but see 11:43 and 12:24d–f).
So the Hebrew reading tradition (Qere); the written text (Ketiv) has “and they came.”
Hebrew “my little one is thicker than my father’s loins.”
Probably whips with barbs or metal tips.
The Septuagint lacks verse 17.
Adoram is a short form of Adoniram (“my lord is exalted”); see 4:6.
The Septuagint reads “one hundred and twenty thousand.”
Shemaiah means “Yahweh has heard.”

The Septuagint adds a long alternative account of Rehoboam’s accession and Jeroboam’s rise and return (12:24a–z). In it Jeroboam’s mother is a prostitute named Sarira, Jeroboam marries Ano, the sister of Pharaoh’s wife, the story of his sick son (compare 14:1–18) comes before the assembly at Shechem, and the prophet who tears the garment is Shemaiah rather than Ahijah (compare 11:29–31).
Penuel means “face of God” (Genesis 32:30); it was east of the Jordan on the Jabbok.
So the Septuagint; the Hebrew reads “to them.”
Bethel means “house of God.”
Dan means “judge” or “he judged”; it lay at the northern edge of Israel.
Hebrew “went before the one, as far as Dan.” Some think words have dropped out, such as “to Bethel and before the other.”

Hebrew “in the eighth month,” that is, Bul (6:38), later called Marcheshvan, of the spring-start calendar, one month after the Feast of Booths in Judah (8:2). The exact modern dates varied with the lunar calendar.

verses.text: And behold, a man of God came out of Judah by the word of Yahweh to Bethel, while Jeroboam was standing by the altar to burn incense.

By the word of Yahweh he cried out against the altar: “Altar, altar, this is what Yahweh says: ‘A son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah{a} by name. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who burn incense on you, and human bones will be burned on you.’ ”
That same day he gave a sign: “This is the sign that Yahweh has spoken: the altar will be split apart, and the ashes on it will be poured out.”

When King Jeroboam heard what the man of God had cried out against the altar in Bethel, he thrust out his hand from beside the altar, saying, “Arrest him!” And the hand he had thrust out toward him withered,{b} so that he was unable to pull it back.
The altar also was split apart, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign the man of God had given by the word of Yahweh.

Then the king said to the man of God, “Please seek the favor of Yahweh your God and pray for me, so that my hand is made well again.” So the man of God sought Yahweh’s favor, and the king’s hand was made well again and became as it was before.
Then the king said to the man of God, “Come home with me and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward.”
But the man of God said to the king, “Though you should give me half of your house, I would not go in with you; I will not eat bread or drink water here.
For so I was commanded by the word of Yahweh: ‘Eat no bread, drink no water, and do not go back by the way you came.’ ”
So he left by a different road and did not go back on the road by which he had come to Bethel.
Now an old prophet lived in Bethel. His son{c} came and told him all that the man of God had done that day in Bethel; and the words he had spoken to the king, they told to their father as well.
Their father asked them, “Which way did he go?” His sons had seen{d} the way the man of God who came from Judah had gone.
He said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” So they saddled the donkey for him, and he rode on it.
He went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak. He said to him, “Are you the man of God who came from Judah?” He answered, “I am.”
Then he said to him, “Come home with me and eat some bread.”
He replied, “I may not go back with you or go in with you, and I will not eat bread or drink water with you in this place,
for a word came to me by the word of Yahweh: ‘You shall eat no bread or drink water there, and you shall not return by going the way you came.’ ”
The old man told him, “I am a prophet also, as you are, and an angel said to me by the word of Yahweh, ‘Bring him back home with you to eat bread and drink water.’ ” But he was deceiving him.
So he went back with him and ate bread in his house and drank water.
While they sat at the table, Yahweh’s word came to the prophet who had brought him back,
and he cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah, “This is what Yahweh says: ‘Because you have defied the mouth of Yahweh and have not kept the command that Yahweh your God gave you,
but have come back and eaten bread and drunk water in the place of which he told you, “Eat no bread and drink no water,” your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers.’ ”
After he had eaten bread and drunk, the old prophet saddled the donkey for the prophet he had brought back.
He went on his way, and a lion met him on the road and killed him. His body was flung down in the road; the donkey stood by it, and the lion too stood by the body.
Some men passing by saw the body flung in the road and the lion standing next to it, and they came and told it in the town where the old prophet lived.

When the prophet who had brought him back from the road heard it, he said, “It is the man of God who defied the mouth of Yahweh. Therefore Yahweh has given him to the lion, which has mauled him and killed him, according to the word Yahweh spoke to him.”{e}
He told his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me,” and they saddled it.
He went and found the body thrown on the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or mauled the donkey.
The prophet picked up the body of the man of God, laid it on the donkey, and brought it back. The old prophet came into his town to mourn and to bury him.
He laid the body in his own grave, and they mourned over him, “Alas, my brother!”
When he had buried him, he told his sons, “At my death, bury me in the same tomb as the man of God; place my bones next to his.{f}
For the word he cried out by the word of Yahweh against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines of the high places in the towns of Samaria{g} will surely come to pass.”

Even after this Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way, but again he made priests for the high places from all ranks of the people. Anyone who wished, he ordained{h} to be priests of the high places.
This thing became the sin of the house of Jeroboam, so as to cut it off and destroy it from the face of the earth.

notes.text: Josiah means “Yahweh supports” or “Yahweh heals.” His reign and the fulfillment of this word are told in 2 Kings 22–23 (see 23:15–18).
Hebrew “dried up.”
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint reads “his sons.”
Hebrew “his sons had seen.” The Septuagint reads “his sons showed him.”
The Septuagint lacks most of the second half of verse 26 and all of verse 27.
The Septuagint adds “so that my bones may be preserved with his bones” (compare 2 Kings 23:18).
Samaria, named in 16:24, was not founded until the reign of Omri. The phrase may reflect the later name of the northern region.
Hebrew “he filled his hand.”

verses.text: At that time Abijah{a} son of Jeroboam fell sick.{b}

Jeroboam said to his wife, “Get up and disguise yourself, so that no one will know you are Jeroboam’s wife, and go to Shiloh. Ahijah the prophet lives there, who foretold to me that I would reign over this people.
Take with you ten loaves, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what will become of the boy.”
Jeroboam’s wife did so. She got up and went to Shiloh and came to Ahijah’s house. Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were fixed{c} because of his age.

But Yahweh had said to Ahijah, “Jeroboam’s wife is on her way to inquire of you about her son, since he is ill. Speak to her in this way. On coming in, she will be acting as if she were someone else.”
So when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet as she came in at the door, he said, “Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be someone else? I have been sent to you with hard news.
Go, tell Jeroboam, ‘This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: Because I lifted you up out of the people and made you ruler over my people Israel,

I tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you. Yet you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, doing only what was right in my eyes.
You have done more evil than all who were before you. You have gone and made for yourself other gods and molten images, provoking me to anger, and you have thrown me behind your back.

Therefore I am bringing disaster on the house of Jeroboam. I will cut off from Jeroboam every male,{d} bond or free in Israel, and I will sweep away the house of Jeroboam as one sweeps away dung, until it is all gone.
Whoever of Jeroboam’s line dies in the city, dogs shall devour; whoever dies in the field, the birds of the sky shall devour. For Yahweh has spoken.’
As for you, get up and go home. When your feet enter the city, the child will die.

All Israel will mourn for him and bury him. He alone of Jeroboam’s family will come to a grave, because in him something pleasing to Yahweh, the God of Israel, has been found in the house of Jeroboam.
And Yahweh will raise up for himself a king over Israel who will cut off the house of Jeroboam on that day. What then? Even now!{e}

Yahweh will strike Israel, as a reed is shaken in the water, and he will root Israel up out of this good land that he gave their fathers and disperse them beyond the Euphrates,{f} because they have made their Asherah poles,{g} provoking Yahweh to anger.
He will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he committed and which he caused Israel to commit.”
Then Jeroboam’s wife got up and left and came to Tirzah.{h} As she crossed the threshold of the house, the child died.
They buried him, and all Israel mourned for him, according to the word of Yahweh, which he spoke through his servant Ahijah the prophet.
The rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he made war and how he reigned, are written in the Book of the Chronicles{i} of the Kings of Israel.
Jeroboam reigned twenty-two years. Then he slept with his fathers, and Nadab{j} his son reigned in his place.

Meanwhile Rehoboam son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city Yahweh had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother’s name was Naamah{k} the Ammonite.
Judah did what was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and by the sins they committed they provoked him to jealousy beyond all that their fathers had done.
For they also built for themselves high places, sacred stone pillars, and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree.
There were also male shrine prostitutes{l} in the land. They did according to all the abominations of the nations that Yahweh had driven out before the Israelites.
In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem.
He took away the treasures of the house of Yahweh and the treasures of the king’s house; he took everything. He also took all the gold shields that Solomon had made.{m}
So King Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place and committed them to the care of the commanders of the guard,{n} who kept the door of the king’s house.
As often as the king went into the house of Yahweh, the guard carried them and then brought them back to the guardroom.
The rest of the acts of Rehoboam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.
Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Abijam{o} his son reigned in his place.

notes.text: Abijah means “Yahweh is my father.”
The Septuagint lacks verses 1–20 here; a different form of the story of the sick child appears in its addition at 12:24g–n.
Hebrew “had stood,” that is, had become rigid or sightless.
Hebrew “every one who urinates against a wall,” a coarse idiom for males.
Hebrew “And what? Even now.” The meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew “the River.”
Asherah poles were wooden cult objects associated with the Canaanite goddess Asherah.
Tirzah means “pleasantness” or “delight.” It served as the capital of the northern kingdom until Omri built Samaria (16:23–24).
Hebrew “the Book of the Matters of the Days,” the official royal annals, here and throughout Kings.
Nadab means “generous” or “willing.”
Naamah means “pleasant” or “lovely.” In the Septuagint, chapter 14 begins at this verse.
Hebrew qadesh, “consecrated one,” probably a male prostitute associated with a shrine. The Septuagint reads “a conspiracy.”
The Septuagint adds “and the golden spears that David took from the hand of the sons of Hadadezer king of Zobah and brought to Jerusalem” (compare 2 Samuel 8:7).
Hebrew “the runners.”
So the Hebrew here; 2 Chronicles 12:16 reads Abijah. Abijam may mean “my father is Yam” (“sea”), or it may be a variant form of Abijah. The Septuagint reads Abiu.

verses.text: In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijam became king over Judah.
He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah,{a} daughter of Abishalom.{b}
He walked in all the sins that his father had committed before him, and his heart was not wholly true to Yahweh his God, as the heart of David his forefather had been.
Nevertheless, for David’s sake Yahweh his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, raising up his son after him and establishing Jerusalem,
because David had done what was right in Yahweh’s eyes and had not turned aside from anything he commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.{c}
There was war between Rehoboam{d} and Jeroboam all the days of his life.
The rest of the acts of Abijam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? There was war between Abijam and Jeroboam.
Abijam slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa{e} his son reigned in his place.{f}
In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel,{g} Asa began to reign over Judah,
Forty-one years he reigned in Jerusalem. His grandmother{h} was named Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom.
Asa did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes, as David his forefather had done.
He drove the male shrine prostitutes out of the land and removed all the idols{i} that his fathers had made.
He even removed Maacah his grandmother from being queen mother, because she had made an abominable image{j} for Asherah. Asa cut down her image and burned it in the Kidron Valley.{k}
But the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless, Asa’s heart was wholly true to Yahweh all his days.
He brought into the house of Yahweh the holy things his father had dedicated and his own dedicated gifts: silver, gold, and vessels.
There was war between Asa and Baasha{l} king of Israel all their days.
Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and fortified Ramah,{m} to keep anyone from going out or coming in to Asa king of Judah.

Then Asa took all the silver and gold left in the treasure stores of Yahweh’s house and of the king’s house and gave it into the hands of his servants. King Asa sent them to Damascus, to the king of Aram, Ben-hadad{n} son of Tabrimmon, son of Hezion, with this message:

“Let us make a treaty, you and I, like the one between my father and yours. Here I have sent you a present of silver and gold. Go, break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me.”
Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the towns of Israel. He conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all Chinneroth,{o} with all the land of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah and stayed in Tirzah.

Then King Asa made a proclamation to all Judah; none was exempt. They carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them King Asa fortified Geba{p} of Benjamin and Mizpah.{q}

The rest of all the acts of Asa, all his might, all that he did, and the towns he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? But in his old age he was diseased in his feet.
Asa slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father. And Jehoshaphat{r} his son reigned in his place.
Nadab son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel two years.
He did what was evil in Yahweh’s sight and walked in the way of his father and in his sin, which he caused Israel to commit.

Baasha son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him, and Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon,{s} which belonged to the Philistines, while Nadab and all Israel were laying siege to Gibbethon.
So Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and reigned in his place.

As soon as he was king, he struck down all the house of Jeroboam. He left to Jeroboam not one that breathed, until he had destroyed it, according to the word of Yahweh that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite,
because of the sins of Jeroboam that he committed and that he caused Israel to commit, and because of the provocation with which he provoked Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger.
The rest of the acts of Nadab and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.{t}
In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king in Tirzah over all Israel, for twenty-four years.
He did what was evil in Yahweh’s sight and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin, which he caused Israel to commit.

notes.text: Maacah means “oppression” or perhaps “dull.” 2 Chronicles 13:2 calls Abijah’s mother Micaiah daughter of Uriel of Gibeah.
Abishalom (“my father is peace”) is a form of Absalom (2 Chronicles 11:20–21).
The Septuagint lacks “except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.”
So the Hebrew. Many interpreters think “Abijam” is meant (compare verse 7). The Septuagint lacks verse 6.
Asa may mean “healer.”
The Septuagint adds “in the twenty-fourth year of Jeroboam.”
The Septuagint reads “In the twenty-fourth year of Jeroboam.” The regnal numbers in Kings are given as they stand in the Hebrew.
Hebrew “His mother’s,” here in the sense of grandmother (compare verse 2). The Septuagint calls her Ana.
Hebrew gillulim, a contemptuous word for idols, perhaps “dung pellets.”
Hebrew miphletseth, “a thing to shudder at.” The exact meaning is uncertain.
Kidron perhaps means “dark” or “turbid.” The valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives.
Baasha’s name is of uncertain meaning.
Ramah means “height.” It lay about 5 miles (8 kilometers) north of Jerusalem.
Ben-hadad means “son of Hadad,” the Aramean storm god.
Chinneroth is the region of the Sea of Galilee (Kinnereth, perhaps “lyre-shaped”).
Geba means “hill.”
Mizpah means “watchtower” or “lookout.”
Jehoshaphat means “Yahweh has judged.”
Gibbethon means “height” or “mound.”
The Septuagint lacks verse 32, which repeats verse 16.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh came to Jehu{a} son of Hanani against Baasha:

“Since I lifted you up out of the dust and made you ruler over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have caused my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins,
I am about to sweep away Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat.
Anyone of Baasha’s who dies in the city, the dogs will eat; and anyone of his who dies in the open country, the birds of the sky will eat.”
The rest of the acts of Baasha, what he did and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried in Tirzah. And Elah{b} his son reigned in his place.

Moreover, through the prophet Jehu son of Hanani the word of Yahweh came against Baasha and his house, both because of all the evil he did in Yahweh’s sight, provoking him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he struck it down.{c}
In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah son of Baasha began to reign over Israel at Tirzah, and he reigned two years.{d}
Now Zimri,{e} his servant, who commanded half of his chariot force, formed a plot against him. While Elah was in Tirzah, drinking until drunk at the home of Arza, the palace steward in Tirzah,
Zimri came in and struck him down and killed him, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place.
As soon as he began to reign, when he had taken his seat on his throne, he struck down all the house of Baasha. He did not leave him a single male, whether of his relatives or of his friends.
So Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the word of Yahweh that he spoke against Baasha through Jehu the prophet,

because of all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, which they committed and which they caused Israel to commit, provoking Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols.{f}
The rest of the acts of Elah and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days at Tirzah. The army was encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines,
and the troops in the camp got word: “Zimri has plotted against the king and struck him down.” So that day in the camp all Israel made Omri,{g} the commander of the army, king over Israel.
Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah.
When Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king’s house and burned the king’s house over himself with fire, and so he died,
because of the sins he had committed, doing what was evil in Yahweh’s sight, walking in the way of Jeroboam and in the sin he committed, causing Israel to sin.
The rest of the acts of Zimri, and the conspiracy he carried out, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts. Half of the people followed Tibni son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri.
But Omri’s followers proved stronger than the followers of Tibni son of Ginath. Tibni died,{h} and Omri reigned.
In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel, and he reigned twelve years; six years he reigned in Tirzah.

He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for about 150 pounds of silver,{i} and he built a city on the hill and called the name of the city he built Samaria,{j} after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill.
Omri did what was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and he did more evil than all who were before him.
He walked in all the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in his sins, which he caused Israel to commit, provoking Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols.
The rest of the acts of Omri that he did, and the might he showed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria. And Ahab{k} his son reigned in his place.{l}
In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab son of Omri began to reign over Israel, and Ahab son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years.{m}
And Ahab son of Omri did evil in Yahweh’s sight, more than all who were before him.

As if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, he took as his wife Jezebel,{n} daughter of Ethbaal{o} king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal{p} and bowed down to him.
He set up an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he built in Samaria.
Ahab also made an Asherah pole. Ahab did more to provoke Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him.

In his days Hiel{q} of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of Yahweh that he spoke through Joshua son of Nun.{r}

notes.text: Jehu means “Yahweh is he.” Hanani means “gracious.”
Elah means “terebinth” or “oak.”
That is, because Baasha destroyed the house of Jeroboam (15:29).
The Septuagint lacks the regnal synchronism in this verse, as in verses 10 and 15.
Zimri may mean “my protection” or “my praise.”
Hebrew hebel, “breath, vapor,” often used of idols as empty and futile.
Omri’s name is of uncertain meaning. Assyrian records later call Israel “the house of Omri.”
The Septuagint adds “and Joram his brother at that time.”
Hebrew “two talents of silver,” about 68 kilograms. A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).
Hebrew Shomron, related to Shemer and perhaps meaning “watch hill.” The Septuagint has Semeron.
Ahab means “father’s brother.”
The Septuagint adds here (16:28a–h) an account of the reign of Jehoshaphat of Judah, parallel to 22:41–50, dating his accession to the eleventh year of Omri.
The Septuagint reads “In the second year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah.” The regnal synchronisms are translated as they stand in the Hebrew.
Jezebel may mean “Where is the prince?”, a cry from the worship of Baal; the Hebrew vowels may have been altered to suggest zebel, “dung.”
Ethbaal means “with Baal” or “Baal exists.”
Baal means “lord” or “master,” the title of the Canaanite storm god.
Hiel means “God lives” or “brother of God.”
See Joshua 6:26.

verses.text: Now Elijah{a} the Tishbite, of the settlers of Gilead,{b} said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except by my word.”
Then the word of Yahweh came to him:
“Leave this place, head east, and hide by the Wadi Cherith,{c} facing the Jordan.
You will drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”
So he went and did according to the word of Yahweh. He went and stayed by the Wadi Cherith, east of the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening,{d} and he drank from the brook.
After a while the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land.
Then the word of Yahweh came to him:
“Get up, go to Zarephath,{e} which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. I have commanded a widow there to provide for you.”

So he got up and went to Zarephath. When he came to the gate of the town, a widow was there gathering sticks. He called to her and said, “Please bring me a little water in a jar, so that I may drink.”
As she was going to get it, he called to her and said, “Please bring me a bit of bread in your hand.”

But she said, “As Yahweh your God lives, I have no bread, just a fistful of flour in the jar and a little oil in the jug. Look, I am picking up two sticks to go in and make it ready for my son and myself, so we can eat it and then die.”
Elijah said to her, “Do not be afraid. Go and do as you have said. But first make me a little cake from it and bring it out to me, and afterward make something for yourself and your son.
For Yahweh, the God of Israel, says this: ‘The flour in the jar shall not run out, nor the oil in the jug fail, until the day Yahweh sends rain on the face of the ground.’ ”
She went and did what Elijah told her, and there was food for her, for him, and for her household many days.
The flour in the jar did not run out, nor did the oil in the jug fail, according to the word of Yahweh that he spoke through Elijah.
After these things the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became ill. His illness grew so severe that no breath was left in him.
She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, man of God?{f} Have you come to me to bring my sin to remembrance and to kill my son?”
He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him from her bosom, carried him up to the upper room where he lodged, and laid him down on his own bed.
Then he cried out to Yahweh, “Yahweh my God, have you also brought calamity on the widow with whom I am staying, by killing her son?”
Then he stretched himself out on the child three times and cried out to Yahweh, “Yahweh my God, please let this child’s life{g} come back into him.”
Yahweh listened to the voice of Elijah, and the child’s life came back into him, and he revived.
Elijah picked up the child and carried him down from the upper room into the house and gave him to his mother. And Elijah said, “See, your son is alive.”
The woman said to Elijah, “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of Yahweh in your mouth is truth.”

notes.text: Elijah means “my God is Yahweh” (Hebrew Eliyyahu).

Hebrew mittoshabe gil‘ad, “of the settlers of Gilead.” The Septuagint reads “of Tishbe in Gilead,” reading the same consonants as a place name. Gilead, the hill country east of the Jordan, may mean “rugged” or “heap of witness.”
Cherith perhaps means “cutting” or “ravine.” A wadi is a streambed that is dry except in the rainy season.
The Septuagint reads “bread in the morning and meat in the evening.”
Zarephath means “smelting place.” It lay on the coast between Tyre and Sidon.
Hebrew “What to me and to you?”, an idiom of protest or distancing.
Hebrew nephesh, “soul, life, breath.”

verses.text: After many days the word of Yahweh came to Elijah, in the third year: “Go, show yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain on the face of the ground.”
So Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. The famine was severe in Samaria.
Ahab called Obadiah,{a} who was over the household. (Obadiah feared Yahweh greatly.
When Jezebel was killing off the prophets of Yahweh, Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them, fifty to a cave, and supplied them with bread and water.)
Ahab said to Obadiah, “Go through the land to all the springs of water and to all the wadis. Perhaps we may find grass and keep the horses and mules alive, so that we do not lose all the animals.”
So they divided the land between them to pass through it. Ahab went one way by himself, and Obadiah went another way by himself.
As Obadiah was on the way, there was Elijah coming to meet him. Obadiah recognized him, fell on his face, and said, “Is it you, my lord Elijah?”
He answered him, “It is I. Go, tell your lord, ‘Elijah is here.’ ”
Obadiah said, “What sin have I committed, that you would hand your servant over to Ahab to put me to death?
As Yahweh your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent to look for you. When they said, ‘He is not here,’ he made the kingdom or nation swear that they had not found you.
And now you say, ‘Go, tell your lord, “Elijah is here.” ’

As soon as I leave you, the Spirit of Yahweh will carry you I do not know where. Then when I come and tell Ahab and he cannot find you, he will kill me, though I your servant have feared Yahweh from my youth.
Has my lord not been told what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of Yahweh, how I hid a hundred of Yahweh’s prophets, fifty to a cave, and supplied them with bread and water?
And now you say, ‘Go, tell your lord, “Elijah is here,” ’ and he will kill me.”
Elijah said, “As Yahweh of hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will certainly show myself to him today.”
So Obadiah went to meet Ahab and told him, and Ahab went to meet Elijah.
When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, “Is that you, you troubler of Israel?”
He answered, “It is not I who have brought trouble on Israel. You and your father’s family have done it, by forsaking what Yahweh commanded and going after the Baals.
Now then, summon all Israel to meet me at Mount Carmel,{b} along with Baal’s four hundred fifty prophets and Asherah’s four hundred prophets, the ones Jezebel feeds at her table.”
So Ahab sent word among all the Israelites and gathered the prophets together at Mount Carmel.
Elijah came near to all the people and said, “How long will you limp between two opinions?{c} If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, follow him.” But the people answered him not a word.
Then Elijah said to the people, “I, I alone, am left as a prophet of Yahweh, but Baal’s prophets are four hundred and fifty men.{d}
Have them give us two bulls. They may pick one bull, cut it up, and set it on the wood without lighting any fire. I will make the second bull ready, set it on the wood, and light no fire either.
Then you call on the name of your god, and I will call on the name of Yahweh. The God who answers by fire, he is God.” And all the people answered, “Well spoken.”{e}
Then Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, “Choose one bull for yourselves and prepare it first, for you are many. Call on the name of your god, but put no fire to it.”

So they took the bull that was given them and made it ready, and from morning to noon they kept calling on Baal’s name: “Baal, answer us!” But not a sound came, and no one answered. And they limped about the altar they had made.
At noon Elijah mocked them, saying, “Call out louder, for he is a god! Perhaps he is deep in thought, or he has gone aside,{f} or he is on a journey. Perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened.”
So they cried out louder and cut themselves with swords and spears, as was their custom, until the blood gushed out over them.
When midday had passed, they raved on{g} until the time of the offering of the evening grain offering,{h} yet there was no sound, no answer, no one listening.
Then Elijah said to all the people, “Come near to me.” All the people came near to him, and he repaired the altar of Yahweh that had been torn down.
Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of Yahweh had come, saying, “Israel shall be your name.”
With the stones he built an altar in the name of Yahweh. He made a trench around the altar large enough to hold about 4 gallons of seed.{i}
He arranged the wood, cut the bull in pieces, and laid it on the wood. Then he said, “Fill four jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and on the wood.”
He said, “Again,” and they did it again. He said, “A third time,” and they did it a third time.
The water ran around the altar, and he filled the trench also with water.

At the time of the offering of the evening grain offering, Elijah the prophet came near and said, “Yahweh, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known today that you are God in Israel, and that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things at your word.
Answer me, Yahweh, answer me, so that this people may know that you, Yahweh, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back again.”
Then the fire of Yahweh fell and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.
When all the people saw it, they fell on their faces and said, “Yahweh, he is God! Yahweh, he is God!”
Elijah said to them, “Seize the prophets of Baal. Do not let one of them escape.” They seized them, and Elijah brought them down to the Wadi Kishon{j} and slaughtered them there.
Then Elijah said to Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a roaring rain.”
So Ahab went up to eat and drink. Elijah went up to the top of Carmel, bowed himself down on the ground, and put his face between his knees.
He said to his servant, “Go up now and look toward the sea.” He went up and looked and said, “There is nothing.” Seven times Elijah said, “Go again.”

The seventh time he said, “Look, a cloud as small as a man’s hand is rising from the sea.” Elijah said, “Go up and say to Ahab, ‘Harness your chariot and go down, so that the rain does not stop you.’ ”
In a little while the sky grew black with clouds and wind, and a downpour came. Ahab got in his chariot and headed for Jezreel.{k}
But the hand of Yahweh was on Elijah. He tucked up his robe{l} and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to the entrance of Jezreel.

notes.text: Obadiah means “servant of Yahweh.” The Septuagint calls him Abdiu.
Carmel means “garden land” or “orchard.” The mountain ridge runs from the Mediterranean coast near modern Haifa toward the southeast.
Hebrew “between the two branches” or “crutches.” The Septuagint reads “halt on both feet.”
The Septuagint adds “and the prophets of the Asherah, four hundred.”
Hebrew “The word is good.”
Probably a euphemism for relieving himself.
Hebrew “they prophesied,” here of frenzied ecstatic behavior.

Hebrew “until the going up of the minchah.” The evening grain offering was made in the late afternoon, about 3 p.m. Here the Septuagint adds “and Elijah spoke to the prophets of the abominations, saying, ‘Stand aside now, and I will offer my burnt offering.’ ”

Hebrew “as great as a house of two seahs of seed,” either a trench holding two seahs (about 15 liters) of seed, or one enclosing an area that two seahs of seed would sow. A seah was about 7 quarts (about 7.3 liters).
Kishon may mean “winding.” It drains the Jezreel Valley to the sea north of Carmel.
Jezreel means “God sows.”
Hebrew “he girded his loins.”

verses.text: Ahab told Jezebel everything Elijah had done, and how he had put all the prophets to the sword.
Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying,{a} “May the gods deal with me, and worse, if by this hour tomorrow I have not done to your life what was done to each of theirs.”
He was afraid,{b} and he got up and fled for his life. He came to Beersheba,{c} which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there.

But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness. He came and sat down under a broom bush{d} and asked that he might die. “It is enough,” he said. “Now, Yahweh, take my life, for I am no better than my ancestors.”
He lay down and fell asleep under the broom bush. Suddenly an angel touched him and said to him, “Get up and eat.”
He looked, and near his head lay a loaf baked on heated stones, and a jar of water. After eating and drinking, he lay down once more.
The angel of Yahweh came back a second time and touched him. “Get up and eat,” he said, “or the journey will be beyond your strength.”
He got up, ate and drank, and in the strength of that food he walked forty days and forty nights to Horeb,{e} the mountain of God.
There he came to a cave and spent the night. And the word of Yahweh came to him, and he said to him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He answered, “I have been very zealous for Yahweh, the God of hosts. The Israelites have forsaken your covenant; they have torn down your altars and put your prophets to death by the sword. I am the only one left, and now they want my life too.”

He said, “Go out and stand on the mountain before Yahweh.” And look, Yahweh was passing by. A great and mighty wind was tearing the mountains apart and shattering the rocks before Yahweh, but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake, but Yahweh was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake came a fire, but Yahweh was not in the fire. And after the fire, the sound of a thin silence.{f}
When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak, went out, and stood at the cave’s entrance. And a voice came to him: “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He answered, “I have been very zealous for Yahweh, the God of hosts. The Israelites have forsaken your covenant; they have torn down your altars and put your prophets to death by the sword. I am the only one left, and now they want my life too.”
Yahweh said to him, “Go back the way you came, to the wilderness of Damascus. When you get there, anoint Hazael{g} to be king of Aram.
Anoint also Jehu{h} the son of Nimshi to be king of Israel, and anoint Elisha{i} the son of Shaphat, from Abel-meholah,{j} to succeed you as prophet.
Anyone who gets away from Hazael’s sword Jehu will put to death, and anyone who gets away from Jehu’s sword Elisha will put to death.
Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal and every mouth that has not kissed him.”
So he went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat. He was plowing; twelve pairs of oxen went before him, and he drove the last. Elijah crossed over to him and flung his cloak on him.
Elisha left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back. What have I done to you?”{k}

Elisha turned back from following him, took the yoke of oxen, and slaughtered them. He boiled their meat using the oxen’s gear for fuel and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he got up, followed Elijah, and served him.

notes.text: The Septuagint begins Jezebel’s message, “If you are Elijah and I am Jezebel, …”
So the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses. The Masoretic text vocalizes the consonants as “He saw.”
Beersheba means “well of seven” or “well of the oath.”
Or “juniper,” as in older translations. The plant is the white broom (retama).
Horeb means “dryness” or “desolation”; it is another name for Mount Sinai.
Or “a gentle whisper,” “a still small voice.” The Septuagint reads “the sound of a gentle breeze.”
Hazael means “God sees.”
Jehu means “Yahweh is he.”
Elisha means “God saves.”
Abel-meholah means “meadow of dancing.”
Or “Go back, for what have I done to you?” The sense is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “Return, for I have done a work for you.”

verses.text: Ben-hadad{a} king of Aram{b} mustered his whole army. Thirty-two kings were with him, with horses and chariots. He went up, laid siege to Samaria, and attacked it.
He sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel with this word: “Thus says Ben-hadad:
‘Your silver and gold belong to me, and the best of your wives and sons belong to me as well.’ ”
The king of Israel replied, “It is as you have said, my lord the king. I and everything I own are yours.”
The messengers came back and said, “This is what Ben-hadad says: ‘I sent you word that you must hand over to me your silver and your gold, your wives and your children.
But about this time tomorrow I will send my servants to you, and they will search your house and your servants’ houses. Whatever pleases your eyes{c} they will lay hands on and carry away.’ ”

Then the king of Israel summoned all the elders of the land and said, “Take note and see how this man is looking for trouble. He demanded my wives and my sons, my silver and my gold, and I held nothing back from him.”
All the elders and all the people said to him, “Do not listen, and do not consent.”

So he told Ben-hadad’s messengers, “Say to my lord the king, ‘Everything you first asked of your servant I will do, but this demand I am unable to meet.’ ” The messengers left and took the answer back.
Ben-hadad sent word to him: “May the gods do so to me and more also, if the dust of Samaria is enough to give a handful to each of the people who follow me.”
The king of Israel answered, “Tell him, ‘The one who straps on his armor should not boast like the one who takes it off.’ ”
When Ben-hadad heard this message, he and the kings were drinking in the booths.{d} He said to his servants, “Take your positions!” And they took their positions against the city.
Then a prophet approached Ahab king of Israel and said, “This is what Yahweh says: ‘Do you see all this great horde? I am giving it into your hand today, and you will know that I am Yahweh.’ ”
Ahab asked, “By whom?” He said, “This is what Yahweh says: ‘By the young men who serve the district governors.’ ” Then he asked, “Who will begin the battle?” He answered, “You.”
So Ahab counted the young men of the district governors; there were 232 of them. After them he counted the whole fighting force of Israel, seven thousand.
They set out at noon. Ben-hadad, meanwhile, was getting drunk in the booths together with the thirty-two kings who had come to help him.
The young men of the district governors led the way out. Ben-hadad had sent men out, and word came back to him: “Some men are coming out of Samaria.”
He said, “If they have come out for peace, take them alive. If they have come out for war, take them alive.”
But these went out from the city, the young men of the district governors and the army behind them,
and each one struck down his man. Aram fled, and Israel pursued them, but Ben-hadad king of Aram escaped on a horse with some horsemen.
The king of Israel went out and struck the horses and chariots, and inflicted a great defeat on Aram.
Then the prophet came to the king of Israel and said to him, “Go, strengthen yourself, and consider well what you must do, because when the year turns{e} Aram’s king will march on you again.”
The servants of the king of Aram said to him, “Their gods are gods of the hills; that is why they were stronger than we. But let us fight them on the plain, and surely we will be stronger than they.
And do this: take every one of the kings out of his command, and appoint governors instead.
Then muster an army like the army you lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot. Let us fight them on the plain, and surely we will be stronger than they.” He listened to their advice and did so.
In the spring Ben-hadad mustered Aram and went up to Aphek{f} to fight against Israel.
The Israelites were mustered and provisioned and went out to meet them. The Israelites camped opposite them like two little flocks of goats, while Aram filled the countryside.

Then the man of God came near and said to the king of Israel, “This is what Yahweh says: ‘Because Aram has said, “Yahweh is a god of the hills but not a god of the valleys,” I will give all this great horde into your hand, and you will know that I am Yahweh.’ ”
They camped facing one another for seven days. On the seventh day the battle was joined, and the Israelites struck down one hundred thousand Aramean foot soldiers in one day.
The rest fled to Aphek, into the city, and the wall collapsed on twenty-seven thousand of the men who remained. Ben-hadad also fled and came into the city, into an inner room.

His servants said to him, “Look, we have heard that the kings of Israel’s house keep faith and show mercy. Let us wrap sackcloth around our waists, put ropes on our heads, and go out to Israel’s king. He may let you live.”

So they tied sackcloth around their waists and ropes on their heads, went to the king of Israel, and said, “Your servant Ben-hadad says, ‘Please let me live.’ ” He said, “Is he still alive? He is my brother.”

The men took this as an omen. They quickly caught it up from him{g} and said, “Yes, your brother Ben-hadad!” He said, “Go and bring him.” Ben-hadad came out to him, and he had him come up into the chariot.

Ben-hadad said to him, “The towns my father took from your father I will give back, and you may set up bazaars{h} for yourself in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria.” Ahab said,{i} “On these terms I will release you.” So he made a treaty with him and let him go.
By the word of Yahweh a certain man of the sons of the prophets{j} said to his companion, “Strike me.” But the man refused to strike him.
Then he said to him, “Because you have not obeyed the voice of Yahweh, as soon as you leave me a lion will kill you.” And when he left him, a lion found him and killed him.
Then he found another man and said, “Strike me.” The man struck him and wounded him.
Then the prophet went and waited for the king by the road, disguising himself with a bandage over his eyes.

As the king passed by, he cried out to the king, “Your servant had gone out into the middle of the fighting. A man stepped aside and brought someone to me and said, ‘Guard this man. If he goes missing, your life will be forfeit for his life, or else you will pay about 75 pounds of silver.’{k}
While your servant was busy here and there, he was gone.” The king of Israel said to him, “That is your sentence; you yourself have decided it.”
Then he quickly removed the bandage from his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets.
He said to the king, “This is what Yahweh says: ‘Because you let slip from your hand the man I had devoted to destruction, your life shall go for his life, and your people for his people.’ ”
The king of Israel went home to Samaria, sullen and angry.

notes.text: The Septuagint places this chapter after the story of Naboth’s vineyard, numbering it chapter 21; its chapter 20 is the Hebrew and English chapter 21. Ben-hadad means “son of Hadad,” the Aramean storm god. The Septuagint renders it “the son of Ader.”
Aram is the land of the Arameans, centered on Damascus; older translations call it Syria, following the Septuagint.
Hebrew “the desire of your eyes.” The Septuagint has “the desirable things of their eyes.”
Hebrew sukkot, temporary shelters of a field camp. The Septuagint reads the place name Succoth at verse 16.
Hebrew “at the return of the year,” the season when kings went to war; likewise in verse 26.
Aphek means “fortress.” Several towns bore the name; this one was probably east of the Sea of Galilee.
The Hebrew of this clause is uncertain.
Hebrew “streets,” probably market quarters for merchants.
Hebrew lacks “Ahab said.”
That is, a member of a prophetic guild.
Hebrew “a talent of silver.” A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).

verses.text: After these things there was the matter of a vineyard belonging to Naboth{a} the Jezreelite. It was in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.{b}
Ahab said to Naboth, “Give me your vineyard to be my vegetable garden, since it lies next to my house. I will trade you a finer vineyard for it, or, if you would rather, pay you its value in silver.”
But Naboth said to Ahab, “Yahweh forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my ancestors.”

Ahab went home sullen and angry over what Naboth the Jezreelite had told him, for he had said, “I will not give you the inheritance of my ancestors.” He lay on his bed, turned his face away, and would not eat.
His wife Jezebel came to him and asked, “Why are you so dispirited that you will not eat?”

He told her, “Because I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and said to him, ‘Let me buy your vineyard for silver, or I will trade you some other vineyard for it, if you would rather.’ But he answered, ‘I will not give you my vineyard.’ ”
His wife Jezebel said to him, “Are you not the one who rules Israel now? Get up, eat something, and cheer up. I will get you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”
So she wrote letters in Ahab’s name, sealed them with his seal, and sent them to the elders and nobles of Naboth’s town, his neighbors there.
This is what the letters said: “Call for a fast and give Naboth a seat of honor before the people.
Put two worthless men{c} across from him, and let them bear witness against him: ‘You have cursed{d} God and the king.’ Then lead him out and stone him until he dies.”
The elders and nobles of Naboth’s town, who lived there with him, carried out Jezebel’s instructions exactly as her letters had directed.
They called for a fast and gave Naboth a seat of honor before the people.

Then the two worthless men came and took their seats across from him and bore witness against Naboth before the people: “Naboth cursed God and the king.” So they took him outside the town and stoned him with stones, and he died.
Then they sent a message to Jezebel: “Naboth was stoned and has died.”

As soon as Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, she said to Ahab, “Get up and take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he would not sell you. Naboth is not living anymore; he is dead.”
When Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, Ahab got up{e} to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite and take possession of it.
Then the word of Yahweh came to Elijah the Tishbite:
“Get up and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria. He is in Naboth’s vineyard, where he has gone to take possession of it.

Tell him, ‘This is what Yahweh says: Have you murdered and also taken possession?’ And tell him, ‘This is what Yahweh says: On the very spot where dogs lapped Naboth’s blood, dogs will lap up your own blood too.’ ”{f}
Ahab said to Elijah, “So you have found me, my enemy?” He answered, “I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do what is evil in the sight of Yahweh.
I am about to bring disaster on you. I will sweep you away and cut off from Ahab every male,{g} slave or free,{h} in Israel.
I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you have provoked me to anger and made Israel sin.
And concerning Jezebel also Yahweh has spoken: ‘The dogs will eat Jezebel by the rampart{i} of Jezreel.’
Whoever of Ahab’s family dies within the city will be eaten by dogs, and whoever dies in the countryside will be eaten by the birds of the sky.”
(There was truly no one like Ahab, who sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of Yahweh, urged on by his wife Jezebel.
He acted most abominably in going after idols,{j} just as the Amorites had done, whom Yahweh drove out before the Israelites.)
When Ahab heard these words, he tore his clothes, put sackcloth on his body, and fasted. He lay in sackcloth and went about subdued.{k}
Then the word of Yahweh came to Elijah the Tishbite:
“Do you see how Ahab has bowed low before me? Since he has bowed low before me, I will hold back the disaster during his lifetime. It is in his son’s time that I will bring ruin on his house.”

notes.text: The Septuagint places this chapter before the account of the Aramean wars (English chapter 20), as its chapter 20. Naboth may mean “sprout” or “fruit.”
The Septuagint reads “near the threshing floor of Ahab king of Samaria” and lacks “in Jezreel.”
Hebrew “sons of Belial,” that is, scoundrels; likewise in verse 13.
Hebrew “blessed,” a scribal euphemism for “cursed”; likewise in verse 13.
The Septuagint adds that Ahab tore his clothes and put on sackcloth, and only afterward got up and went down.

The Septuagint reads “In every place where the swine and the dogs licked the blood of Naboth, there the dogs will lick your blood,” and adds “and the prostitutes will bathe in your blood” (compare 22:38).
Hebrew “every one who urinates against a wall.”
The meaning of the Hebrew pair ‘atsur we‘azub is uncertain: perhaps “bond or free,” or “ruler or helper.”
Hebrew chel, “rampart” or “outer wall.” Compare 2 Kings 9:36, “the plot of ground of Jezreel.”
Hebrew gillulim, a contemptuous term for idols, perhaps “dung pellets.”
Hebrew “softly” or “quietly.” The Septuagint reads “weeping.”

verses.text: Three years went by with no war between Aram and Israel.
In the third year, though, Judah’s king Jehoshaphat{a} came down to visit the king of Israel.
The king of Israel said to his officials, “You know that Ramoth-gilead{b} is ours, don’t you? Yet we sit still and do not take it back from Aram’s king.”
He said to Jehoshaphat, “Will you go with me to battle at Ramoth-gilead?” Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses.”
But Jehoshaphat also said to the king of Israel, “First, please, inquire for the word of Yahweh.”

So the king of Israel assembled the prophets, around four hundred of them, and asked, “Should I march against Ramoth-gilead, or should I refrain?” They said, “Go up, for the Lord{c} will give it into the king’s hand.”
But Jehoshaphat said, “Is there no other prophet of Yahweh here, of whom we may inquire?”

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is still one man through whom we could inquire of Yahweh, Micaiah{d} son of Imlah. But I hate him, because he never prophesies good about me, only evil.” Jehoshaphat said, “The king should not say so.”
So the king of Israel called an officer and said, “Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once.”
Now Israel’s king and Judah’s king Jehoshaphat sat on their thrones in royal robes at the threshing floor by the entry to Samaria’s gate, while all the prophets prophesied in front of them.
Zedekiah{e} son of Chenaanah made himself horns of iron and said, “This is what Yahweh says: ‘With these you will butt the Arameans till you have finished them off.’ ”
All the prophets were prophesying the same: “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph. Yahweh will give it into the king’s hand.”
The messenger sent to call Micaiah told him, “See here, the prophets are all of one voice in speaking favorably to the king. Please make your message agree with theirs and say something good.”
But Micaiah said, “As Yahweh lives, whatever Yahweh says to me, that is what I will speak.”

When he came to the king, the king said to him, “Micaiah, shall we go to battle against Ramoth-gilead, or shall we hold back?” He answered him, “Go up and triumph. Yahweh will give it into the king’s hand.”
But the king said to him, “How often must I put you under oath to say only what is true when you speak to me in Yahweh’s name?”
Then he said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, like sheep that have no shepherd. And Yahweh said, ‘These have no master. Let each of them go home in peace.’ ”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you he would not prophesy good about me, but only evil?”
Micaiah said, “Therefore hear the word of Yahweh. I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne, with all the host of heaven standing beside him, on his right and on his left.
And Yahweh said, ‘Who will entice Ahab, so that he will go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ One said one thing, and another said another.
Then a spirit came forward and stood before Yahweh and said, ‘I will entice him.’
Yahweh asked him, ‘How?’ He said, ‘I will go out and become a deceiving spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.’ Yahweh said, ‘Entice him you shall, and you will succeed. Go out and do it.’
So now, look, Yahweh has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these prophets of yours. Yahweh has decreed disaster for you.”
Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came up, struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said, “Which way did the Spirit of Yahweh pass from me to speak to you?”
Micaiah said, “You will see on the day you go into an inner room to hide.”
The king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah and return him to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king’s son,
and say, ‘This is what the king says: Put this fellow in prison and feed him on short rations of bread and water{f} until I come back safely.’ ”
Micaiah said, “If you ever come back safely, Yahweh has not spoken through me.” And he said, “Listen, all you peoples!”{g}
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will go into the fight in disguise, while you keep your royal robes on.” So Israel’s king disguised himself and entered the battle.
Now the king of Aram had commanded the thirty-two commanders of his chariots, “Fight with no one, small or great, except the king of Israel alone.”
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “Surely that is the king of Israel.” So they turned to fight against him, and Jehoshaphat cried out.
When the chariot commanders saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.

But a man drew his bow without taking aim{h} and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate. He said to his chariot driver, “Turn around and get me out of the fighting,{i} for I am wounded.”
The battle grew fierce that day, and the king was propped up in his chariot facing the Arameans. The blood from the wound ran into the floor of the chariot, and at evening he died.
As the sun was going down, a shout passed through the ranks: “Each man to his own town, each to his own country!”
So the king died and was brought to Samaria, and they buried the king in Samaria.
They washed the chariot by the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked up his blood, and the prostitutes bathed there,{j} according to the word that Yahweh had spoken.
The rest of the acts of Ahab and all that he did, the ivory house he built and all the towns he built, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel?
So Ahab slept with his ancestors, and Ahaziah{k} his son reigned in his place.
Jehoshaphat son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Azubah{l} daughter of Shilhi.

He followed the whole path of Asa his father without swerving from it, doing what pleased Yahweh. Yet the high places were not removed; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.{m}
Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel.
The rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, the might he showed, and how he waged war, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah?
He purged from the land the rest of the male cult prostitutes{n} who remained from the days of his father Asa.{o}
There was no king in Edom; a deputy served as king.
Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish{p} to sail to Ophir for gold, but they never sailed, because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber.
Then Ahaziah son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, “Let my servants go with your servants in the ships,” but Jehoshaphat was not willing.
Then Jehoshaphat slept with his ancestors and was buried beside them in the city of David his father, and Jehoram{q} his son reigned in his place.
Ahaziah son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned two years over Israel.
He did what was evil in the sight of Yahweh and walked in the way of his father and in the way of his mother and in the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin.
He served Baal and worshiped him and provoked Yahweh, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done.

notes.text: Jehoshaphat means “Yahweh has judged.”
Ramoth-gilead means “heights of Gilead.”
Hebrew Adonai.
Micaiah means “Who is like Yahweh?”
Zedekiah means “Yahweh is righteousness.”
Hebrew “bread of affliction and water of affliction.”
These words are identical to the opening of Micah 1:2 and may be a later link between the two prophets named Micah/Micaiah. The Septuagint lacks them.
Hebrew “in his innocence,” that is, at random.
Hebrew “the camp”; the Septuagint reads “the battle.”
Or “they washed the armor.” The Septuagint reads “the swine and the dogs licked up the blood, and the prostitutes washed themselves in the blood.”
Ahaziah means “Yahweh has grasped.”
Azubah means “forsaken.”
In Hebrew this verse is two verses, 43 and 44, so from here to the end of the chapter the Hebrew verse numbers are one higher than the English.
Hebrew qadesh. See the note at 14:24.
The Septuagint lacks verses 46–49. Some of this material appears in its addition at 16:28a–h.
Ships of Tarshish were large seagoing merchant ships. The Ketiv reads “ten ships.”
Jehoram means “Yahweh is exalted.”
